analysis.one_liner: Ends federal tobacco price supports, eliminates the tax deduction for cigarette advertising, and funds anti-smoking and anti-drug programs.
analysis.headline: The bill died in House subcommittees in 1994 without ever getting a vote, leaving the tobacco price support program and the tobacco industry's advertising tax deduction in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have shut down the federal program that props up tobacco prices for growers and guarantees them a market through quotas. It would also have barred tobacco companies from deducting their advertising costs from their taxes, and used about half of the resulting revenue for a government anti-smoking ad campaign and school anti-drug programs. It was sent to four House committees, then to subcommittees, and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would stop underwriting tobacco prices through the federal support program. Public health would gain from a government advertising campaign on the risks of tobacco, and schools would gain funding for anti-drug programs. Tobacco growers would bear the cost of losing price supports and quotas.

how_it_helps.text: Terminates the tobacco price support program and repeals the tobacco marketing quota system, ending a federal program that guarantees growers a minimum price and a share of the market [S2][S3].

Bars tobacco companies from deducting advertising and promotional expenses — broadcast, print, billboard, event sponsorships, brand-name merchandise, and product placement in movies — from their federal income taxes [S3].
Creates an Anti-Tobacco Use Trust Fund funded by half the new tax revenue, split between school anti-drug programs and a public advertising campaign on the health risks of tobacco [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco growers, who would lose the guaranteed minimum price and quota system, and tobacco companies, which would lose a substantial tax write-off and face less-protected leaf prices. Rural tobacco-dependent communities would absorb much of the economic shock. Some portion of the industry's lost tax break could be passed through to smokers in prices.

drawbacks.text: Ending price supports and quotas would eliminate a guaranteed income floor for tobacco farm families and reduce the value of quota holdings, which farmers had treated as a business asset — a real economic hit to rural communities built around tobacco [S2][S3].

The trust fund's revenue depends entirely on how much money the advertising deduction ban raises, an uncertain amount, and half of it is earmarked for school anti-drug programs that have little direct connection to tobacco [S3].

Shutting down the quota system all at once, effective January 1, 1995, would have flooded or disrupted the leaf market with no transition assistance for growers, beyond continuing their existing legal liabilities [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits are real: ending a subsidy program that props up a product that kills, and removing a tax break for promoting it, while funding counter-advertising aimed especially at young people. The costs fall narrowly on tobacco farm communities, and the bill offered them no transition aid, which is the strongest good-faith objection to it. On balance the trade favors the public, but the design was blunt.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees, then to three subcommittees over the summer of 1994, and none of them ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Karan English introduced the bill on June 30, 1994, with nine Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
It was referred jointly to the Committees on Agriculture, Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means [S5].

In July and early August 1994 it was referred to subcommittees on specialty crops, on select education, and on health and the environment, and no further action was ever recorded before the 103rd Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco growers and cigarette manufacturers are better off: the price support and quota program survived, and tobacco advertising remained tax-deductible.

for.name: Rep. Karan English
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

for.name: 9 of 258 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all nine cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, passed it to its Specialty Crops Subcommittee on July 8, 1994, and never reported the bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and Labor Committees
against.what_they_did: Received joint referrals and referred portions to subcommittees; none reported the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only record of support is one sponsor and nine cosponsors, all Democrats, and no recorded opposition actors appear in the record.

industries.note: The bill would terminate the federal price support program and marketing quotas that guarantee growers minimum prices and a protected market share. Growers' interest in keeping that program runs at the expense of taxpayers, who back the support system.

The bill eliminates their tax deduction for virtually all tobacco advertising and promotion, including sponsorships and movie placements, and raises their cost of marketing a product whose health costs fall on the public.
Broadcasters, publishers, billboard firms, and event sponsors would lose tobacco ad and sponsorship dollars that the bill converts to tax revenue.
